quote: Kommen in der Decimalbruchentwicklung für $\pi$ 11 1en {+hintereinander+} in einander vor?
english: Do eleven 1s occur consecutively in the decimal expansion of pi?
topic: The page bounds the genus of algebraic relations between transcendental entire functions, sketches elliptic functions as non-Euclidean geometry on a genus-1 ring with distance as the elliptic integral of the third kind, and asks whether 11 consecutive ones occur in the decimal expansion of pi.

triage.modern_statement: Does the 11-digit string 11111111111 (eleven 1s in a row) appear somewhere in the decimal expansion of π = 3.14159…? A single occurrence would settle it, so a large enough computation can answer it with a yes. No theorem currently guarantees it. The general claim behind it, that every finite digit string appears in π (which would follow if π were 'disjunctive' or normal in base 10), is still unproven.
triage.answered_by: Most likely answered 'yes' by large computer calculations of π's digits in the late 20th or 21st century, possibly the trillion-digit-scale computations by Kanada and later teams. I could not find a source that gives the position of eleven consecutive 1s, so I can't name who found it, when, or where. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Repeated-digit runs in π's digits are tracked and recorded. One example is the run of six 9s starting at decimal place 762 (the 'Feynman point').
MathWorld records where special digit runs first appear in π: 999999 occurs at decimal place 762 and continues as 9999998.
Trillions of digits of π have been computed and published, which is far more than needed to search for any 11-digit string (22.4 trillion digits were available in 2017).
Over 1.24 trillion digits had been computed by December 2002 (Kanada et al.).

triage.why: The question is precise but can only be settled one way by computation: finding the string answers yes, while not finding it proves nothing. If the digits behaved randomly, a specific 11-digit string would appear about once every 10^11 digits. With more than 10^13 digits computed, it would very likely have been found many times. That is only a probability argument, though. My searches confirmed that digit-run statistics are recorded and that trillions of digits exist, but I hit the search limit before finding a page that gives the position of 11111111111. So the 'solved' verdict is an inference, not something a source directly states. The deeper question, whether π is normal or contains every finite string, is famous and still open, but no source here shows it is an active research program in its own right. For high confidence you would need to check a digit-search tool or a record list of digit runs in π.
